catalog.name: Antarctic Data Layers
catalog.description:
Introduction

This catalogue brings observations, geophysical interpretations and numerical model output for Antarctica and the Ross Sea region into one map, so that air temperature, ice sheet change, solid-Earth response and sub-ice geology can be explored together. The layers do not share an evidential status: each one keeps its own methods, units and uncertainty, and should be interpreted with the source metadata linked below.

Data layers provided

AntAir ICE — Antarctic air temperature

A daily snapshot from AntAir ICE, a near-surface air temperature dataset for terrestrial Antarctica, the ice shelves and the seasonal sea ice around Antarctica, on a 1 km grid, available for 2003 to 2021. Air temperature was modelled from MODIS ice surface temperature and land surface temperature using linear models, with in-situ air temperature from 117 automatic weather stations as the response variable.

The source rasters are Antarctic Polar Stereographic (EPSG:3031) and store air temperature in degrees Celsius multiplied by 10, which is why the legend runs from -900 to 0: a value of -300 is -30 ℃. Areas with cloud contamination, and areas without sea ice, are no data.

Explore the AntAir visualisation · Metadata record · Dataset · Nielsen et al. (2023) study · Processing code

P-SKRIPS — coupled atmosphere, sea ice and ocean model

Daily mean fields from P-SKRIPS, a coupled regional model of the Ross Sea region that links the Polar WRF atmospheric model with the MITgcm ocean and sea ice model. Version 1 was developed to conserve heat and mass fluxes fully between the two components, which otherwise lets a regional simulation drift over multiple years.

Four layers are provided, each a daily mean for 1 February 2017: wind speed 10 m above the surface, the same wind as arrows, and air temperature 2 m above the surface in degrees Celsius and in kelvin. Wind speed is derived from the eastward and northward components as sqrt(u² + v²). The arrow layer shows direction and speed and can be placed over the wind speed raster; the Celsius and kelvin layers are the same field in different units.

Explore the P-SKRIPS visualisation · Metadata record · Malyarenko et al. (2023) model study · Model code

Ice sheet and glacial isostatic adjustment model output

Output of the ice sheet and glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA) models behind Lowry et al. (2024), which examined Holocene retreat and readvance of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet. The ice sheet model output covers Antarctic bed topography, ice thickness and an ice sheet mask at 500 year intervals from 9.5 ka to present; the GIA model output is global bed topography at 100 year intervals. GIA is the slow deformation of the solid Earth as it responds to changes in ice load.

Three layers are drawn from this output: modelled ice thickness at 9.5 ka, global bed topography for one GIA run, and a bed topography anomaly, which is derived from that same GIA output by subtraction and so shows a difference in bed elevation rather than an absolute elevation.

Each layer is named after its model run, and the identifiers encode the parameters that were varied: hotf is the Holocene ocean thermal forcing anomaly, mv the mantle viscosity and fr the lithosphere flexural rigidity. The ice sheet layer shown here is run ism_hotf0-0_mv7-5e20_fr1e24 at 9.5 ka; the GIA bed topography layer is run mv1e21_fr1e24_w0p0_weakEarth_t20. Click a point on the ice sheet layer to chart modelled ice thickness through the model time steps, with one line per model run.

These are model results rather than direct measurements. Record the run identifier and the model time whenever results are exported or compared.

Metadata record · Lowry et al. (2024) study · Model output

Ross Ice Shelf basement and sediment thickness

The estimated thickness of non-magnetic sedimentary cover above magnetic basement beneath the Ross Ice Shelf and Ross Embayment. Depth to magnetic basement was determined by Werner deconvolution of ROSETTA-Ice airborne magnetic data, constrained by offshore seismic data tied to the ice shelf with Operation IceBridge airborne magnetic data; sediment thickness was then calculated above that basement using a sub-ice shelf bathymetry model.

This is a geophysical interpretation rather than sampled geology. The source dataset also carries upper and lower uncertainty grids and the flight line profiles behind the solutions, for both Ross Ice Shelf and Ross Embayment extents; quantitative work should use those as well.

Metadata record · Dataset · Tankersley et al. (2022) study · Reproducible workflow · PolarToolkit examples

Experimental 3D ice thickness blocks

A proof of concept derived from one ice sheet model thickness band. Values are rounded upward into 250 m classes and positioned on the ETOPO surface. The columns are illustrative: their tops do not represent a reconstructed physical ice surface, and they should not be used for quantitative reconstruction.

How to use the layers

  • Add one or more layers and read each legend for its units and range.
  • Overlay the P-SKRIPS wind arrows on wind speed to see direction and magnitude together.
  • Use either the Celsius or the kelvin P-SKRIPS temperature layer; they are the same model field.
  • Click the ice sheet layer to chart modelled ice thickness through time and across runs.
  • Quote layer names, run identifiers and dates when saving screenshots or reporting results.

Data and model limitations

  1. The catalogue mixes observations, statistically derived datasets and model simulations. These do not carry the same evidential status or the same kind of uncertainty.
  2. AntAir ICE depends on usable MODIS scenes and on calibration against a sparse weather station network, so cloud cover, season, surface type and location all affect its availability and accuracy.
  3. P-SKRIPS version 1 is one coupled model setup. Its published validation rests on a one month summer and a one month winter experiment designed to demonstrate heat and mass flux conservation, not to establish a long-term observational climatology.
  4. The ice sheet and GIA layers depend on model forcing, Earth rheology, parameter choices, initial conditions and the selected time slice. Compare multiple runs before treating any one result as a preferred reconstruction.
  5. The basement and sediment layer is an interpretation of airborne magnetic data, with its own uncertainty grids.
  6. The experimental 3D blocks are for visual exploration only.

Data access, licensing and citation

All four source datasets are published through the New Zealand Antarctic Data Catalogue (AntCAT) under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence, which requires attribution. Use the metadata records linked above to obtain the original files, and cite both the dataset and the related study when publishing analysis based on these layers.

  • Bendix Nielsen, E., Katurji, M., Zawar-Reza, P., Meyer, H. (2023). Antarctic Daily Mesoscale Air Temperature Dataset Derived from Remotely Sensed Land and Ice Surface Temperature – AntAir ICE. PANGAEA. https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.954750
  • Malyarenko, A., Gossart, A. (2023). P-SKRIPS Version 1. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7739059
  • Lowry, D. P., Han, H. K., Golledge, N. R., Gomez, N., Johnson, K. M., McKay, R. M. (2024). Ocean cavity regime shift reversed West Antarctic grounding line retreat in the late Holocene. Nature Communications, 15, 3176. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47369-3
  • Tankersley, M. D., Horgan, H. J., Siddoway, C. S., Caratori Tontini, F., Tinto, K. J. (2022). Basement topography and sediment thickness beneath Antarctica's Ross Ice Shelf. Geophysical Research Letters, 49, e2021GL097371. https://doi.org/10.1029/2021GL097371

These layers are published by the Geospatial Research Institute Toi Hangarau, University of Canterbury, on the EDDIE digital twin platform. The institute hosts and presents the layers; it does not own the source datasets. Email: gri-enquiries@canterbury.ac.nz.

Contact

Source data custodian: the datasets are held in the New Zealand Antarctic Data Catalogue; use the contact details in each metadata record linked above.

Dashboard and technical contact: Geospatial Research Institute Toi Hangarau, University of Canterbury, https://geospatial.ac.nz/. Email: gri-enquiries@canterbury.ac.nz.

Consult the original data, metadata, uncertainty products and publications before quantitative, operational or safety-critical use.

catalog.name: Sea ice forecast
catalog.description:
Introduction

An eight week forecast of Antarctic sea ice concentration, one map per week. Concentration is the fraction of each 1 degree model cell covered by sea ice, from 0 for open water to 1 for complete cover. The legend shows it as a percentage, in bands from under 15% to 80-100%, and cells below 1% are left clear.

Key findings

The forecast comes from the first graph neural network framework for weekly Antarctic sea ice concentration and its anomalies on subseasonal time scales of up to eight weeks ahead, developed by Tobias Milz, Varvara Vetrova and Marwan Katurji at the University of Canterbury. Benchmarked against five convolutional neural network architectures, two statistical baselines and the operational ECMWF S2S dynamical forecast, it achieved the lowest error on three of four metrics, cutting full-grid mean absolute error by roughly 18% relative to the strongest convolutional benchmark and by 48% relative to a persistence forecast, while using 4 to 24 times fewer trainable parameters. Only on root-mean-square error at the ice edge did it fall behind, by about 4%. A feature attribution analysis identified sea surface temperature as the dominant driver of its predictions beyond the seasonal climatology.

Forecast provided

One map is available for each of the eight forecast weeks, and each week's layer is titled with that week's date. A new forecast is generated every Monday at 03:00 New Zealand time.

Open the process below, select a week and a display, and run it; then click the resulting map to chart all eight forecast weeks at that location. Raw 1° cells draws one value per 1 degree model cell, as the model produces it. Smoothed blends between neighbouring cells. The chart follows the display chosen for the map.

Data and model setup

The model forecasts from the previous four weeks of conditions. Sea ice concentration for each live forecast comes from the near-real-time NOAA/NSIDC climate data record of passive microwave sea ice concentration (G10016, version 4), distributed by the National Snow and Ice Data Center. The model was trained on the historical record (NSIDC-0051, version 2), which shares the same 25 km polar stereographic grid, together with ERA5 reanalysis.

Atmospheric and ocean predictors come from ERA5, produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts and distributed through the Copernicus Climate Data Store: the 10 m eastward and northward wind components, 2 m air temperature, mean sea level pressure, total precipitation, sea surface temperature and the land-sea mask. Alongside these the model is given sea ice concentration and its departure from the historical day-of-year climatology it was trained against.

Contributions and data ownership

  • Forecast model: Tobias Milz and Marwan Katurji, School of Earth and Environment, and Varvara Vetrova, School of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Canterbury. The graph neural network and its training code are their work, and this dashboard runs that code as written.
  • Dashboard and platform: Geospatial Research Institute Toi Hangarau, University of Canterbury, built on the EDDIE digital twin platform. The institute publishes this forecast layer; it does not own the forecast model or the source data.
  • Sea ice observations: NSIDC distributes both the near-real-time record that drives each forecast and the historical record the model was trained on, produced from Nimbus-7 SMMR and DMSP SSM/I-SSMIS passive microwave data. NSIDC and the source data providers retain stewardship of those products.
  • Environmental predictors: ERA5 is produced by ECMWF and distributed by the Copernicus Climate Data Store, under the Copernicus CC-BY licence terms.
  • Research support: the New Zealand Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment through the TAIAO programme (CONT-64517-SSIFDS-UOW) and the Antarctic Science Platform (ANTARCTICANZ2504).
  • Ownership: publishing this forecast transfers no ownership of the model, NSIDC or ERA5 data. Each source remains subject to its provider's citation and licence terms.

Model limitations

  1. The forecast is deterministic: it carries no uncertainty range.
  2. The 1 degree grid does not resolve narrow leads or small coastal features.
  3. It forecasts concentration only, not ice thickness, drift or navigational safety.
  4. Forecast skill generally decreases with lead time.
  5. The forecast is not land-masked. Land and coastal cells are supplied to the model as zero concentration, so any value drawn over land carries no meaning.

Study, data and licences

Milz, T., Vetrova, V., Katurji, M. (2026). Graph neural networks for Antarctic sea ice concentration forecasting. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70984-7. Published online 16 September 2026 and free to read under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 licence; at the time of writing this is the accepted manuscript, to be replaced by the final version of record.

The source data require their own citations:

  • Meier, W. N., Fetterer, F., Windnagel, A. K., Stewart, J. S., Stafford, T. (2026). Near-Real-Time NOAA/NSIDC Climate Data Record of Passive Microwave Sea Ice Concentration (G10016, Version 4). Boulder, Colorado USA. National Snow and Ice Data Center. https://doi.org/10.7265/tm2n-1m33
  • DiGirolamo, N., Parkinson, C. L., Cavalieri, D. J., Gloersen, P., Zwally, H. J. (2022). Sea Ice Concentrations from Nimbus-7 SMMR and DMSP SSM/I-SSMIS Passive Microwave Data (NSIDC-0051, Version 2). Boulder, Colorado USA. NASA National Snow and Ice Data Center Distributed Active Archive Center. https://doi.org/10.5067/MPYG15WAA4WX
  • ERA5 hourly data on single levels from 1940 to present. Copernicus Climate Data Store, under the CC-BY licence. https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.adbb2d47
